claim: Tumors often co-exist with T cells that recognize somatically mutated peptides presented by cancer cells on major histocompatibility complex I (MHC-I).
source: Tumors often co-exist with T cells that recognize somatically mutated peptides presented by cancer cells on major histocompatibility complex I (MHC-I).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about tumor immunology.

claim: Immunogenic tumor antigens do not lead to immune-mediated cell rejection when the fraction of cells bearing each antigen ('clonal fraction') is low.
source: Surprisingly, we show that immunogenic tumor antigens do not lead to immune-mediated cell rejection when the fraction of cells bearing each antigen ('clonal fraction') is low.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experiments described in the manuscript, supported by data from library screens and flow cytometry experiments.

claim: The clonal fraction necessary to lead to rejection of immunogenic tumor subclones depends on the antigen.
source: Moreover, the clonal fraction necessary to lead to rejection of immunogenic tumor subclones depends on the antigen.
evidence: This is a primary finding from experiments showing different rejection thresholds for different antigens (SIINFEKL, TAYRYHLL, SNFVSAGI).

claim: Tumor neoantigen heterogeneity has an underappreciated impact on immune elimination of cancer cells.
source: These data indicate that tumor neoantigen heterogeneity has an underappreciated impact on immune elimination of cancer cells and has implications for the design of immunotherapeutics such as cancer vaccines.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings combined with inference about the broader implications.

claim: Human cancers bear uniquely distinguishable features on the surface of their cells in the form of neoantigens, which are peptides derived from mutated, foreign or oncofetal proteins that are presented in complex with major histocompatibility complex I (MHC-I) molecules.
source: Human cancers bear uniquely distinguishable features on the surface of their cells in the form of neoantigens, which are peptides derived from mutated, foreign or oncofetal proteins that are presented in complex with major histocompatibility complex I (MHC-I) molecules.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about cancer neoantigens.

claim: Neoantigens are short, 8–11 amino acid fragments that specifically mark cancer cells and activate potent immune responses that can lead to effective anti-cancer therapy.
source: These short, 8–11 amino acid fragments specifically mark cancer cells and activate potent immune responses that can lead to effective anti-cancer therapy (Tran et al., 2014; Rosenberg and Restifo, 2015; Zacharakis et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The existence of T cells that recognize neoantigens is often not sufficient to eliminate tumors.
source: Yet, the existence of T cells that recognize neoantigens is often not sufficient to eliminate tumors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the paradox of tumor immunity.

claim: Karl Hellström first described the coexistence of tumor-specific lymphocytes together with cancer cells in human solid tumors as a paradox 50 years ago.
source: Karl Hellström first described the coexistence of tumor-specific lymphocytes together with cancer cells in human solid tumors as a paradox 50 years ago (Hellström et al., 1968).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation.

claim: Sporadic tumors occurring in aged or carcinogen-treated mice induce strong T cell responses only when transferred into new hosts, thereby preventing engraftment.
source: In mice, an analogously enigmatic observation has been made that sporadic tumors occurring in aged or carcinogen-treated mice induce strong T cell responses only when transferred into new hosts, thereby preventing engraftment (Heike et al., 1994; Dubey et al., 1997; Shankaran et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The increased rate of tumor formation in immunocompromised individuals has led to the hypothesis that the immune system can and does eliminate some tumors, particularly virally induced tumors, before they become clinically apparent.
source: The increased rate of tumor formation in immunocompromised individuals has led to the hypothesis that the immune system can and does eliminate some tumors, particularly virally induced tumors, before they become clinically apparent (Schulz, 2009).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The PresentER antigen minigene is comprised of an endoplasmic reticulum (ER) signal sequence followed by a short peptide/epitope.
source: The PresentER antigen minigene is comprised of an endoplasmic reticulum (ER) signal sequence followed by a short peptide/epitope.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental system developed by the authors.

claim: Expression of the peptide and its display on MHC-I does not require proteasomal degradation or peptide processing, thus enabling precise definition of the exact epitope displayed to the immune system.
source: Expression of the peptide and its display on MHC-I does not require proteasomal degradation or peptide processing, thus enabling precise definition of the exact epitope displayed to the immune system.
evidence: This is a description of the PresentER system's mechanism and advantage.

claim: Transporter associated with antigen presentation (Tap) deficient cell lines expressing PresentER antigen minigenes lead to surface presentation of the encoded MHC-I peptide, detectable by multiple modalities, including fluorescently labeled antibodies directed to specific MHC-I ligands, mass spectrometry based immunopeptidomics and antigen-specific T cell reactivity.
source: As previously described (Gejman, 2018a), Transporter associated with antigen presentation (Tap) deficient cell lines expressing PresentER antigen minigenes lead to surface presentation of the encoded MHC-I peptide, detectable by multiple modalities, including fluorescently labeled antibodies directed to specific MHC-I ligands, mass spectrometry based immunopeptidomics and antigen-specific T cell reactivity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and describes experimental validation.

claim: Endogenously expressed MHC-I tumor antigens are presented on the cell surface at several hundred to several thousand sites per cell.
source: Previously we, and others, had shown that endogenously expressed MHC-I tumor antigens are presented on the cell surface at several hundred to several thousand sites per cell (Dao et al., 2013; Sergeeva et al., 2011; Mathias et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There were on average 3500 binding sites per RMA/S cell expressing PresentER-SIINFEKL.
source: Using a radiolabeled TCR mimic antibody (25-D1.16) reactive with SIINFEKL/H-2Kb, we demonstrated that there were on average 3500 binding sites per RMA/S cell expressing PresentER-SIINFEKL, compared with ~90 sites on cells expressing PresentER-MSIIFFLPL, suggesting that the PresentER system allows display of the epitopes in a relatively physiologic range.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from radioimmunoassay experiments.

claim: Tumors expressing known non-immunogenic peptides grew, while tumors expressing known immunogenic peptides were rejected in some or most animals.
source: Tumors expressing known non-immunogenic peptides grew, while tumors expressing known immunogenic peptides were rejected in some or most animals (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from in vivo tumor experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At 7 days after tumor injection, T cells specific for the chicken ovalbumin peptide SIINFEKL could be detected in tumor draining lymph nodes of animals injected with PresentER-SIINFEKL expressing cells.
source: At 7 days after tumor injection, T cells specific for the chicken ovalbumin peptide SIINFEKL could be detected in tumor draining lymph nodes of animals injected with PresentER-SIINFEKL expressing cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Haemotoxylin and Eosin (H and E) staining of regressing PresentER-SIINFEKL tumors showed lymphocytic infiltration with hyalin rich fibrin deposits, indicating cell death.
source: Haemotoxylin and Eosin (H and E) staining of regressing PresentER-SIINFEKL tumors showed lymphocytic infiltration with hyalin rich fibrin deposits, indicating cell death.
evidence: This is a histological observation from H&E staining.

claim: Tumors with PresentER-FEKIILSN (a non-MHC-I binding peptide) were well-vascularized, highly cellular and with trace lymphocytic infiltration.
source: By contrast, tumors with PresentER-FEKIILSN (a non-MHC-I binding peptide) were well-vascularized, highly cellular and with trace lymphocytic infiltration (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a histological observation from H&E staining shown in Figure 1D.

claim: SIINFEKL tumors were not rejected in Rag-/- animals.
source: In order to verify that the mechanism of tumor rejection was indeed T cell dependent, we injected Rag-/- animals with SIINFEKL or FEKIILSN positive tumors and confirmed that SIINFEKL tumors were not rejected (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from tumor growth experiments in Rag-/- mice shown in Figure 1E.

claim: RMA/S tumors expressing PresentER antigen minigenes can recapitulate the known immunogenicity of individual mouse MHC-I ligands in a T cell dependent manner.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that RMA/S tumors expressing PresentER antigen minigenes can recapitulate the known immunogenicity of individual mouse MHC-I ligands in a T cell dependent manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The immunogenic SIINFEKL, SIYRYYGL and TAYRYHLL expressing tumors were rejected, but the non-immunogenic FEKIILSN, EQYKFYSV and TWHRYHLL tumors found on the contralateral flank were not.
source: The immunogenic SIINFEKL, SIYRYYGL and TAYRYHLL expressing tumors were rejected, but the non-immunogenic FEKIILSN, EQYKFYSV and TWHRYHLL tumors found on the contralateral flank were not (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from dual-flank tumor experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Tumor rejection is local and an effective immune response to an immunogenic tumor does not affect the growth of a non-immunogenic tumor.
source: This suggests that tumor rejection is local and that an effective immune response to an immunogenic tumor does not affect the growth of a non-immunogenic tumor.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the dual-flank tumor experiments.

claim: In tumors where PresentER-SIINFEKL cells were greater than 25% of a tumor, tumors were smaller and tumor rejection occurred more frequently, especially when tumors were comprised of ≥50% immunogenic cells.
source: In tumors where PresentER-SIINFEKL cells were greater than 25% of a tumor, tumors were smaller and tumor rejection occurred more frequently, especially when tumors were comprised of ≥50% immunogenic cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from mixed tumor experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Within a non-immunogenic (eGFP labeled) tumor, immunogenic (mCherry labeled) sub-populations were eliminated.
source: Remarkably, within a non-immunogenic (eGFP labeled) tumor, immunogenic (mCherry labeled) sub-populations were eliminated (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from flow cytometry analysis of mixed tumors shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The immune system is capable of recognizing and selectively depleting immunogenic tumor subclones within the context of a largely non-immunogenic tumor.
source: Thus, in this model, the immune system is capable of recognizing and selectively depleting immunogenic tumor subclones within the context of a largely non-immunogenic tumor.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mixed tumor experiments.

claim: Immunoediting in vivo leading to loss of tumor clones with immunogenic neoantigen-encoding mutations has previously been observed in syngeneic mouse tumor models.
source: Immunoediting in vivo leading to loss of tumor clones with immunogenic neoantigen-encoding mutations has previously been observed in syngeneic mouse tumor models (Matsushita et al., 2012; DuPage et al., 2012; DuPage et al., 2011), suggesting that this approach might be viable.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: No minigenes were robustly depleted during growth in vivo in the library screen.
source: Comparison of minigene abundance in the tumor outgrowth with minigene abundance in the pre-tumor samples led to the surprising finding that no minigenes were robustly depleted during growth in vivo (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the library screen experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Minigenes that were abundant in the library at time of injection maintained their abundance despite in vivo growth of the tumor.
source: Some minigenes that were not abundant in the library (<1/10,000) at the time of injection were depleted or dropped out entirely in the tumor due simply to stochastic drop-out; however, minigenes that were abundant in the library at time of injection maintained their abundance despite in vivo growth of the tumor.
evidence: This is an observation from the library screen data analysis.

claim: Even positive control minigenes encoding strongly immunogenic peptides were not depleted in the library context.
source: Surprisingly, even positive control minigenes encoding strongly immunogenic peptides (orange points) were not depleted in this context.
evidence: This is a key observation from the library screen experiments.

claim: The immunogenic controls SIINFEKL, VTFVFAGL and SNFVFAGI were found at 0.005–0.013% of cells before injection into mice, which correspond to between 250 and 650 cells injected out of 5 × 10^6.
source: The immunogenic controls SIINFEKL, VTFVFAGL and SNFVFAGI were found at 0.005–0.013% of cells before injection into mice, which correspond to between 250 and 650 cells injected out of 5 × 106.
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of the library composition.

claim: The number of cells expressing the immunogenic antigens upon injection is very low and thus analogous to the number of cells that are present during early tumor development, when immunogenic transformed cells first arise.
source: The number of cells expressing the immunogenic antigens upon injection is very low and thus analogous to the number of cells that are present during early tumor development, when immunogenic transformed cells first arise.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the experimental conditions to early tumorigenesis.

claim: Vaccination with the library yielded detectable T cell populations specific to the immunogenic peptides.
source: Only the immunogenic peptides found in the library showed an increased number of CD44+/tetramer+ CD8 T cells, while the other two peptides did not show significant changes (Figure 4B). Therefore, vaccination with the library yielded detectable T cell populations specific to the immunogenic peptides.
evidence: This is a finding from tetramer staining experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Slower tumor growth was noted in the vaccinated as compared to the non-vaccinated mice.
source: Vaccinated and non-vaccinated mice were then challenged with 5 × 106 RMA/S cells bearing the wild type peptide library. Slower tumor growth was noted in the vaccinated as compared to the non-vaccinated mice, suggesting that a vaccine-related anti-tumor effect may have occurred (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an observation from tumor growth experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Neither vaccinated nor unvaccinated animals showed depletion of immunogenic control minigenes in relation to the non-immunogenic control minigenes.
source: However, neither vaccinated nor unvaccinated animals showed depletion of immunogenic control minigenes in relation to the non-immunogenic control minigenes (Figure 4D–F and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the vaccination and challenge experiments shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: Antigen-specific immunity was not observed in response to prophylactic vaccination in the library setting.
source: Thus, although slower tumor growth was noted, antigen-specific immunity was not observed in response to prophylactic vaccination in the library setting, suggesting a possible response to some other, broadly expressed, cellular antigens not represented in the peptide library.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the vaccination experiments with speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Tumor cells bearing the immunogenic peptides SIINFEKL and TAYRYHLL were depleted when they comprised as little as 1% of the tumor.
source: Relative to their proportion upon engraftment, tumor cells bearing the immunogenic peptides SIINFEKL and TAYRYHLL were depleted when they comprised as little as 1% of the tumor.
evidence: This is a finding from the clonal fraction threshold experiments.

claim: Below 1%, depletion of cells bearing SIINFEKL and TAYRYHLL could not be detected.
source: Below 1%, depletion of cells bearing these two minigenes could not be detected.
evidence: This is a finding from the clonal fraction threshold experiments.

claim: Depletion of cells bearing the SNFVSAGI peptide could be reliably detected at 50% and in some tumors at 10%, however depletion could not be detected when the SNFVSAGI cells were found at less than 10% of the tumor.
source: Depletion of cells bearing the SNFVSAGI peptide could be reliably detected at 50% and in some tumors at 10%, however depletion could not be detected when the SNFVSAGI cells were found at less than 10% of the tumor (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from the clonal fraction threshold experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Immunogenic tumor subclones can persist within a tumor and rejection or persistence is dependent on tumor cell percentage of the total tumor mass during tumorigenesis, and not immunogenicity of the cell alone.
source: These findings are surprising, as they indicate that immunogenic tumor subclones can persist within a tumor and that rejection or persistence is dependent on tumor cell percentage of the total tumor mass during tumorigenesis, and not immunogenicity of the cell alone.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the clonal fraction threshold experiments.

claim: Robust depletion of cells bearing immunogenic peptide minigenes did not occur when tumor material was transferred from Rag-/- mice to WT mice.
source: After 17 days, the transferred tumors were harvested and sequenced. Once again, as we observed in both naive and vaccinated mice, robust depletion of cells bearing immunogenic peptide minigenes did not occur.
evidence: This is a finding from the tumor transfer experiments.

claim: Overall minigene abundance was highly correlated between the tumor material transferred and the tumors harvested 17 days later in both WT and Rag-/- mice and in both the wild type and mutant libraries.
source: Overall minigene abundance was highly correlated between the tumor material transferred and the tumors harvested 17 days later in both WT and Rag-/- mice and in both the wild type and mutant libraries (Figure 5D and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the tumor transfer experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: It is the percentage of tumor cells bearing each antigen within a tumor and not the total quantity of antigen that determines if an effective immune response occurs.
source: These results reveal that it is the percentage of tumor cells bearing each antigen within a tumor and not the total quantity of antigen that determines if an effective immune response occurs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the tumor transfer experiments.

claim: The immune system is capable of recognizing cancer cells as foreign based on the presentation of altered or unusual MHC-I ligands on the surface of tumor cells.
source: The immune system is capable of recognizing cancer cells as foreign based on the presentation of altered or unusual MHC-I ligands on the surface of tumor cells—a phenomenon that has been leveraged for cancer therapies such as immune checkpoint blockade and adoptive cell transfer (Tran et al., 2014; Rosenberg and Restifo, 2015; Zacharakis et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The immune system fails to clear immunogenic, clinically detected tumors on its own.
source: Despite this, the immune system fails to clear immunogenic, clinically detected tumors on its own, as has been paradoxically noted for decades (Hellström et al., 1968).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: There is epidemiologic evidence that immunocompromised patients develop more tumors, suggesting that the immune system may prevent some tumors from ever manifesting clinically.
source: There is epidemiologic evidence that immunocompromised patients develop more tumors, suggesting that the immune system may prevent some tumors from ever manifesting clinically.
evidence: This is established knowledge with inference about immune surveillance.

claim: Mutations accumulate at high rates in sun-damaged, but otherwise normal, tissue at levels comparable to cancer cells.
source: However, recent data also suggests that mutations accumulate at high rates in sun-damaged, but otherwise normal, tissue at levels comparable to cancer cells (Martincorena et al., 2015) and that tumors face overall little negative selective pressure (Martincorena et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Tumors face overall little negative selective pressure.
source: However, recent data also suggests that mutations accumulate at high rates in sun-damaged, but otherwise normal, tissue at levels comparable to cancer cells (Martincorena et al., 2015) and that tumors face overall little negative selective pressure (Martincorena et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Immune escape by loss of MHC, when it occurs, is a late and subclonal event.
source: Indeed, immune escape by loss of MHC (Masuda et al., 2007; Cabrera et al., 2000; Gudmundsdóttir et al., 2000; So et al., 2005; Shukla et al., 2015), when it occurs, is a late and subclonal event (McGranahan et al., 2017; Turajlic et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: If T cell surveillance were highly effective during early tumor development, negative selective pressure would be notable in the evolutionary trajectories of tumors and HLA loss would be expected to occur early, frequently and in a clonal manner.
source: If T cell surveillance were highly effective during early tumor development, negative selective pressure would be notable in the evolutionary trajectories of tumors and HLA loss would be expected to occur early, frequently and in a clonal manner.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what would be expected if immune surveillance were highly effective.

claim: Routine T cell immunosurveillance of nascent cancer cells does occur, but is limited by unknown factors, and recognition of tumors as foreign occurs mostly later in tumor development.
source: We interpret the data from human and animal experiments to suggest that routine T cell immunosurveillance of nascent cancer cells does occur, but is limited by unknown factors, and that recognition of tumors as foreign occurs mostly later in tumor development.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data with speculation about the timing of immune recognition.

claim: Tumor heterogeneity is an explicit factor leading to failure of effective immunity in a tumor.
source: Here we report the first evidence that tumor heterogeneity is an explicit factor leading to failure of effective immunity in a tumor and that the maximum level of heterogeneity tolerable before immune escape occurs is dependent on the antigen.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the experimental findings.

claim: The maximum level of heterogeneity tolerable before immune escape occurs is dependent on the antigen.
source: Here we report the first evidence that tumor heterogeneity is an explicit factor leading to failure of effective immunity in a tumor and that the maximum level of heterogeneity tolerable before immune escape occurs is dependent on the antigen.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the experimental findings.

claim: Immune checkpoints or active tumor suppression do not explain the observed immune evasion because such mechanisms would be expected to suppress T cell killing irrespective of the fraction of tumor cells that expresses an immunogenic epitope.
source: Immune checkpoints or active tumor suppression do not explain the observed immune evasion because such mechanisms would be expected to suppress T cell killing irrespective of the fraction of tumor cells that expresses an immunogenic epitope.
evidence: This is a logical inference ruling out alternative explanations.

claim: Low levels of antigen presentation may lead to ineffective cross-presentation of antigen in the tumor draining lymph node, thus limiting T cell activation.
source: Low levels of antigen presentation may lead to ineffective cross-presentation of antigen in the tumor draining lymph node, thus limiting T cell activation (Spiotto et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism supported by citation.

claim: Low levels of immunogenic epitopes of oncogenic drivers presented on transformed cells early during tumorigenesis (at the premalignant stage) were shown to induce a program of cellular hypo-responsiveness in tumor-specific (oncogene-specific) CD8 T cells.
source: In animal models, low levels of immunogenic epitopes of oncogenic drivers presented on transformed cells early during tumorigenesis (at the premalignant stage) were shown to induce a program of cellular hypo-responsiveness in tumor-specific (oncogene-specific) CD8 T cells (Willimsky and Blankenstein, 2005; Schietinger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The mechanism of immune escape in this model is either ineffective T cell activation or failure of activated T cells to identify and kill antigen-positive cells present at low abundance within a sea of cells displaying irrelevant antigens.
source: We speculate that the mechanism of immune escape in this model is either ineffective T cell activation or failure of activated T cells to identify and kill antigen-positive cells present at low abundance within a sea of cells displaying irrelevant antigens.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: Tumors with high mutation burdens respond well to checkpoint blockade.
source: Tumors with high mutation burdens—which are more likely to have immunogenic neoantigens (Van Allen et al., 2015; Yarchoan et al., 2017; Snyder et al., 2014)—and tumors that have mismatch repair (MMR) deficiency or microsatellite instability (MSI-H) respond well to checkpoint blockade (Le et al., 2015; Le et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Tumors that have mismatch repair (MMR) deficiency or microsatellite instability (MSI-H) respond well to checkpoint blockade.
source: Tumors with high mutation burdens—which are more likely to have immunogenic neoantigens (Van Allen et al., 2015; Yarchoan et al., 2017; Snyder et al., 2014)—and tumors that have mismatch repair (MMR) deficiency or microsatellite instability (MSI-H) respond well to checkpoint blockade (Le et al., 2015; Le et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Syngeneic tumors with MMR gene knock outs accumulate mutations over time and grow more slowly in wild type mice than do tumors without MMR deficiency.
source: In mouse models, syngeneic tumors with MMR gene knock outs accumulate mutations over time and grow more slowly in wild type mice than do tumors without MMR deficiency.
evidence: This is established knowledge from mouse models.

claim: Cell lines derived by sub-cloning of MMR deficient lines grow more slowly or are rejected entirely.
source: Cell lines derived by sub-cloning of MMR deficient lines—thus increasing the clonal fractions of each neoantigen—grow more slowly or are rejected entirely.
evidence: This is established knowledge from mouse models.

claim: MMR inactivation in tumors leads to better responses to checkpoint blockade than the parental tumors.
source: In all cases, MMR inactivation in tumors leads to better responses to checkpoint blockade than the parental tumors (Germano et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Survival is inversely related to tumor neoantigen clonality in human patients with lung adenocarcinoma.
source: Moreover, survival is inversely related to tumor neoantigen clonality in human patients with lung adenocarcinoma (McGranahan et al., 2016; Reuben et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Patients whose tumors bear high numbers of subclonal (or branched) neoantigens have increased levels of relapse and worse survival than those patients with more homogenous tumors.
source: Patients whose tumors bear high numbers of subclonal (or branched) neoantigens have increased levels of relapse and worse survival than those patients with more homogenous tumors (McGranahan et al., 2016; Reuben et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Response to checkpoint blockade in lung and skin tumors is associated with lower levels of intratumoral heterogeneity.
source: Response to checkpoint blockade in lung and skin tumors is also associated with lower levels of intratumoral heterogeneity (McGranahan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: While total neoantigen burden is important for long term survival and response to checkpoint blockade, neoantigen clonality is an additional important factor in mediating tumor regression.
source: The combination of these data are highly suggestive that while total neoantigen burden is important for long term survival and response to checkpoint blockade, neoantigen clonality is an additional important factor in mediating tumor regression.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from multiple cited studies.

claim: The discovery that intratumoral heterogeneity prevents effective T cell responses has implications for the development of therapeutic cancer vaccines, checkpoint blockade, adoptive T cell therapies, and studies of tumor immunogenicity.
source: The discovery that intratumoral heterogeneity prevents effective T cell responses has implications for the development of therapeutic cancer vaccines, checkpoint blockade, adoptive T cell therapies, and studies of tumor immunogenicity.
evidence: This is an inference about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: Subclones with very low clonal fraction yet distinct intratumoral functions may be important to tumor survival and growth.
source: For instance, recent data shows that subclones with very low clonal fraction yet distinct intratumoral functions may be important to tumor survival and growth (Vinci et al., 2018)—suggesting that even low abundance tumor subclones may be important targets for immunotherapy.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Even low abundance tumor subclones may be important targets for immunotherapy.
source: For instance, recent data shows that subclones with very low clonal fraction yet distinct intratumoral functions may be important to tumor survival and growth (Vinci et al., 2018)—suggesting that even low abundance tumor subclones may be important targets for immunotherapy.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from cited research.

claim: Small early cancers generally do not bear immunogenic epitopes derived from their limited number of driver oncogenic proteins and few passenger mutations.
source: In general, we may speculate on one mechanism for cancer escape and progression, in which small early cancers generally do not bear immunogenic epitopes derived from their limited number of driver oncogenic proteins and few passenger mutations.
evidence: This is speculation about a mechanism of cancer escape.

claim: As tumors evolve, the neoantigens appearing in subclones do not reach a clonal fraction high enough to breach their antigen-specific immunogenicity thresholds, thereby allowing escape of these otherwise immunogenic clones.
source: Then as the tumors evolve, the neoantigens appearing in subclones do not reach a clonal fraction high enough to breach their antigen-specific immunogenicity thresholds, thereby allowing escape of these otherwise immunogenic clones.
evidence: This is speculation about a mechanism of cancer escape based on the experimental findings.

claim: Sun-damaged and aged healthy tissue is replete with mutations, sometimes reaching frequencies seen in human cancers.
source: This model may help to explain why sun-damaged and aged healthy tissue is replete with mutations, sometimes reaching frequencies seen in human cancers (Martincorena et al., 2015; Risques and Kennedy, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Effective T cell immunity is restrained in the context of healthy tissue and growing tumors.
source: Cumulatively, these findings suggest that effective T cell immunity is restrained in the context of healthy tissue and growing tumors and paint a picture of T cell immunogenicity that is poorly captured by existing models of tissue immunosurveillance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and cited research.
